tracks.title: Nine a.m., and nobody's home
tracks.text: Lesson eight point three — schedules. A sub-lesson, under workflows. Nine a.m., and nobody's home. Here is a line in a plan. SCHEDULED… angle bracket… twenty twenty-six, dash zero six, dash one three… oh nine hundred… plus one w… close bracket. It says, plainly — every Friday at nine. And on Friday at nine, the file just sits on a disk. A few kilobytes of text… doing what text always does. Nothing. [curious] A text file cannot fire itself. Something outside it has to wake up, read the line, and act. The old answer is cron — a daemon reading a table of times. But cron is a fourth unreviewable system. It lives somewhere else, one person edits it, and it can only ever do what its line says — blind to whether the line still makes sense. So this lesson owns two questions. First… what exactly can you write on a headline. Second… what actually wakes up and runs it.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A schedule is two halves of one idea. First half — declared time in the plan. Org timestamps and a schedule property, which the kernel compiles into pure data. Second half — the keeper. An engine-side heartbeat that runs an agent on a cadence, so the declared time gets honored. And here's the thing that matters most. They are not the same clock. Declared time lives in the plan and never fires anything — the kernel parses it, surfaces it, and stops. Cadence time lives in the keeper… the engine that actually ticks. The keeper is not a cron daemon reading your timestamps. It's a metronome that runs an agent… and the agent reads the plan. Hold that split. The whole lesson hangs on it.

tracks.title: One character decides everything
tracks.text: One character decides everything. An org timestamp's first character is its whole meaning. Angle brackets make it active — a thing to act on. Square brackets make it inactive — a thing merely recorded, an event that happened. Anything else parses to nothing. The difference between an appointment… and a diary entry… is one bracket. Inside the brackets, order doesn't matter — the kernel recognizes each token by its shape. First… a ten-character token with a dash at position four is the date. Second… a token with a colon is the time. Third… a token starting with plus, dot-plus, or plus-plus is the repeater. Day names like Friday match none of those shapes, so they fall through and are silently ignored. Let me read you what the parser actually produces. Write angle-bracket, twenty twenty-six dash zero six dash one three, Friday, oh nine hundred, plus one w… and you get — at, twenty twenty-six T oh nine hundred… repeat, plus one w… active, true. Notice the Friday is gone, the time joined the date with a T, and active is true because of the angle brackets. Now switch to square brackets around a date and time, and only one thing changes — active flips to false. Same date… different verb. And one more thing. The repeater is carried raw. Plus one w is just a string the kernel hands forward. It recognizes the prefix… it does not compute the next date. We'll be honest about that later.

tracks.title: When a timestamp isn't enough
tracks.text: When a timestamp isn't enough. Sometimes a repeating timestamp isn't dense enough, and you want a cron expression. For that there's a property — schedule — in the headline's drawer. And it outranks the timestamp. Picture the decision the kernel walks when it asks a headline for its schedule. First it checks — is there a schedule property? If yes, the schedule is a cron object holding that raw string, and we're done. If no, it checks — is there a SCHEDULED timestamp? If yes, the schedule is that timestamp's data. And if neither… the schedule is simply null. So a schedule property of zero six star star star wins, even with a timestamp right beside it — the cron property is the louder voice. One caution. The kernel does not parse or validate that string. Schedule, anything at all… becomes cron, anything at all. It is carried data, not interpreted instruction. And this schedule rides the compiled world — every workflow and sub-workflow carries its own schedule field, surfaced in the run records, queryable like any other structure in the tree.

tracks.title: A metronome, not a cron daemon
tracks.text: [excited] A metronome, not a cron daemon. Here's the bigger realization — the one the whole page turns on. The engine that fires schedules is called the keeper. And it is not crond reading your timestamps. It's a metronome. Each beat, it does one thing — run an agent definition. Then it records the outcome and schedules the next beat. The agent is what reads the plan, sees what's due, and does it. Why a metronome and not a daemon reading the line directly? Because a cron daemon can only do what the line literally says. An agent woken on a tick can read the whole plan in one pass and notice three things at once — a deadline slipped, a dependency just unblocked, and a schedule arrived. Let me walk you through one beat. The keeper wakes. If gitops is on, it first pulls the tenant's git origin — so a push to GitHub becomes live within one tick. Then it runs the agent definition, in the tenant's own repository. The agent reads the plan, does its work, and commits. And because the workdir is that public repo… the keeper's commits are the changelog. Finally the agent reports an outcome, and the keeper schedules the next beat. Declared time is for the plan. Cadence time is for the worker. And the worker is smart enough to reconcile them.

tracks.title: Anatomy of a tick
tracks.text: Anatomy of a tick. A single beat has more rigor than run-a-thing-on-a-timer suggests, because the keeper has to survive restarts, crashes, and runs that hang. Four properties define one beat. First — catch-up scheduling. The last-run time is persisted to disk. On restart, the first delay is the larger of sixty seconds, or the interval minus the time already elapsed. A restart must not reset the rhythm. Second — the wall-clock kill. Every run executes in a linked task with a hard timeout, fifteen minutes by default. Past it, the run is killed outright… and because the worker traps exits, a hung run never takes the worker down with it. Third — the four outcomes. Done… failed… killed… and no-work. These drive what happens next. And fourth — the gitops pull before each run, where a merge conflict aborts and is left for a human, rather than resolved blindly. [curious] The worker is built to keep its rhythm no matter what the run does.

tracks.title: The breather and the backoff
tracks.text: The breather and the backoff. A keeper runs in one of two modes. Interval mode ticks on a fixed cadence — hourly by default. Continuous mode drops the fixed wait and takes a short breather between ticks — forty-five seconds. But continuous-by-default has an obvious failure. An idle agent… burning a model call every forty-five seconds… just to say there's nothing to do. The fix is the no-work protocol and an exponential backoff. When the agent has nothing to do, it begins its final answer with the word NO-WORK. The keeper counts consecutive no-work ticks and backs off, doubling each time, capped at thirty minutes. Let me give you the shape of it. Do real work, and the next tick is forty-five seconds — the breather. One no-work in a row… one minute. Two… two minutes. Three… four. Four… eight. Five… sixteen. And six or more, it settles at the cap — thirty minutes. An idle keeper drifts to one wake every half hour. But the moment there's real work, a single done snaps it straight back to a forty-five-second beat. [chuckles] It stops burning calls on an empty backlog without you lifting a finger. And turning a keeper on is just a handful of environment variables — a keeper def, which is required, no def means no ticks… an interval… continuous mode and its breather… a run timeout… an optional lifecycle… and the tenant whose repo the commits land in.

tracks.title: One manifest, many workers
tracks.text: One manifest, many workers. One keeper runs one agent. To run several on their own cadences, you point a crew variable at a manifest — an org file where each heading is an agent and its drawer is the config. Let me read you a real one. First heading… wren. Its drawer says — def, slash data slash agents slash writer dot org. Lifecycle, a writer lifecycle file. Interval, ten minutes. Second heading… moss. Def, the editor file. Interval, twenty minutes. Each heading becomes one supervised worker. The def is required — a member without it is skipped and logged. The lifecycle is optional. The interval takes ten m, two h, ninety s, or bare milliseconds, defaulting to an hour. Now two things keep a crew from stampeding. First — the stagger. Picture the supervisor starting its workers. Wren ticks first at zero seconds. Moss waits thirty. A third worker waits sixty. They overlap on the wire, but they don't all wake at once. Second — the gate. It admits at most two runs at a time and queues the rest. So wren and moss acquire the gate and run… while a third worker sits queued until one finishes. Each worker releases the gate even on a crash, so a wedged worker can never starve the others. And one last truth — when two agents could grab the same task, the runtime does not lock it. Claiming is a convention the agents follow — a board state change and an agent property, committed to git before the work. The runtime only isolates runs and throttles concurrency.

tracks.title: Declaring what a tick is
tracks.text: Declaring what a tick is. So far a tick has been opaque — just run the agent. A lifecycle makes the cadence itself declarative. A deterministic state machine, written in native org, that runs one transition per tick. The skeleton is deterministic — what the agent does inside a state stays open-ended. Each heading is a state. Its kind is either wake, which runs the agent, or rem, which dreams with no agent. Repeat holds the state for N successful ticks. Next names the successor. And min-interval is a time gate. Let me trace the canonical loop as a story. The agent wakes to add — three times. Then it wakes once to audit what it added. Then it enters a rem state to dream — but only after ten real minutes have passed. Then it wakes to plan… and loops back to adding. The stepping rules are precise. A done increments the hit count, and at the repeat limit it takes the next state and resets. A no-work collapses the remaining repeats and takes the next state now — a fast-forward of repeats only, never a skip. Every state in the declared order still runs, so audits and dreams keep their cadence. And a failed or killed run holds the position and retries the same state next tick — the cadence position is never lost. The position survives restarts, and the spec is re-read every tick… so a hot edit is picked up on the very next beat.

tracks.title: Where it bites
tracks.text: Where it bites — and this one corrects something. Repeater prefixes are recognized, not computed. The kernel sees that plus one w, dot-plus one d, and plus-plus one w are repeaters, and carries them as strings — but no code distinguishes their meanings. That plus shifts by the interval, plus-plus shifts to the future, dot-plus measures from the completion date. Those meanings live in the agent's understanding of org, never in engine code. The cron string, likewise, is uninterpreted data. Now the correction. The parent lesson said a passed deadline is a fact the validator reports. Here's the truth — the validator checks dependency-graph facts, missing languages and dangling inputs. Not time facts. Overdue is arithmetic the reader runs on the parsed headlines… not a diagnostic the kernel emits. And keeper time is at-least, never at-most. A plus one w at nine o'clock does not fire at nine sharp — it fires within a tick of it, when an agent next wakes. Min-interval means no earlier than, never exactly at. The engine's own durations only know seconds, minutes, and hours — no days or weeks. And last — cadence is not autonomy. A keeper makes follow-through cheap. It does not make judgment optional. The pitch is never software that runs itself. Direction stays human. The keeper is just the part that shows up on time.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Will plus one w fire at exactly nine? No — within a tick of it. The keeper wakes an agent on a cadence, and the agent reads the plan and acts on what's due. Nine o'clock means the first tick at or after nine. What's the difference between plus, dot-plus, and plus-plus? In org convention — plus shifts by the interval, plus-plus jumps to the next future date, dot-plus measures from completion. But the kernel only recognizes the prefix and carries the string. The agent honors the meaning. SCHEDULED versus DEADLINE? Scheduled is an appointment — when to start. Deadline is a due date — when it's owed. Only scheduled feeds the headline's schedule, and overdue is arithmetic you run. Keeper or external cron — when each? The keeper is for internal-only control planes a public cron can't reach. When you can reach the endpoint, a triggered drain is leaner — any scheduler hits it, and no poller idles on an empty backlog. Do crew agents fight over tasks? The runtime isolates runs and caps concurrency, but it does not lock tasks — claiming is a convention, committed to git before the work. And what survives a redeploy? Two small files — the last-run timestamp, so the cadence clock isn't reset… and the lifecycle position. A redeploy resumes the rhythm, rather than restarting it.

tracks.title: Back up to the parents
tracks.text: So that's schedules. Two halves of one idea. Declared time, compiled to honest data in the plan — and a keeper, an engine-side heartbeat that gives agents the ticks to honor it. The plan is at-least, never at-most… and never software that runs itself. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This sub-lesson stands on its parent — workflows, lesson eight — for the plan that holds the time. And it leans on agents… for the worker the keeper actually runs. Everything the keeper does… is built from those two.
